subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Dinosaur Extinction
description: A quick, practical guide to The Dinosaur Extinction.

hook.text: 66 million years ago, a 10-kilometer asteroid hit what is now Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula.

buildup.text: The impact released energy equivalent to 10 billion nuclear bombs. Fires swept continents.

discovery.text: Dust and soot blocked sunlight for months. Photosynthesis stopped. Food chains collapsed.

twist.text: 75% of all species died — but small mammals, birds, and crocodiles survived the darkness.

climax.text: Without that asteroid, mammals may never have dominated. Humans might never have evolved.

punchline.text: The worst day in Earth's history made our existence possible.

quiz.question: What percentage of species went extinct in the asteroid impact?

details.summary: The end-Cretaceous extinction 66 million years ago was triggered by an asteroid impact at Chicxulub, Mexico, combined with massive volcanism in India's Deccan Traps. It wiped out all non-avian dinosaurs and roughly 75 percent of all species on Earth.
details.whyItMatters: The dinosaur extinction shows that life on Earth is vulnerable to sudden catastrophic events. It also reveals how ecosystems can recover and diversify after mass extinction.
takeaways: The Chicxulub asteroid was roughly 10 km in diameter
Impact winter blocked sunlight and collapsed food chains globally
Mammals diversified rapidly to fill vacated ecological niches

faq.question: How did the asteroid kill species thousands of miles away?
faq.answer: The impact launched debris into the atmosphere that blocked sunlight for months, collapsing photosynthesis on land and in oceans. Global fires, acid rain, and a prolonged impact winter destroyed food chains far from the crater.

faq.question: Why did mammals survive when dinosaurs did not?
faq.answer: Small-bodied mammals needed less food, could shelter underground or in burrows, and many were omnivores or insectivores able to exploit surviving food sources. Larger, specialized dinosaurs were more vulnerable to food-chain collapse.
